name: The Hall That Is A Corridor
symptom: A house described as a centre-hall or centre-passage plan whose hall is 3 ft 6 in to 4 ft 6 in wide - a corridor with doors in it. There is nowhere to stand aside, nowhere to put a chair or a case clock, and two people meeting in it have to turn sideways. In the eighteenth-century houses it is copied from, the same space was 10 to 14 ft wide and was furnished, used and sometimes danced in.

cause.explanation: Circulation is the only area on a plan that is priced as pure loss: it appears in the square-foot total, it costs the same per foot to build as a bedroom, and it cannot be named in a listing. Every plan review therefore squeezes it, and the code gives a floor to squeeze to - the residential minimum hallway is 36 in - so 42 to 48 in reads as generous. The result is a plan whose parti is named for a room it no longer contains.
cause.cost_saved: Narrowing a 32 ft long passage from 12 ft to 4 ft returns about 256 sq ft to the rooms either side: $45,000-$75,000 of saleable area on a production house, which is why this is the least negotiable fault in the corpus.

rule_violated.statement: At 10 to 14 ft the passage is wider than most modern bedrooms. It is not a corridor; it was furnished and used as a room.

rule_violated.ref: room-vernacular / circulation_parti.width = part * 6 = 6 ft, range 3-10 ft
rule_violated.statement: Measured central passages run 6 to 12 ft: 8-10 ft where the passage is a living space in hot climates, 6-7 ft where it is only circulation. If the design is southern and the passage is 6 ft, the plan has been drawn from a northern precedent.

rule_violated.ref: IRC R311.6 - hallway width not less than 3 ft
rule_violated.statement: The code minimum is a life-safety floor, not a design dimension, and a plan that lands on it has been dimensioned by the code rather than by the type.
Roughly one third of a five-bay front; one fifth to one quarter of a seven-bay. The passage is a bay of the elevation, not a gap between bays.

correct_practice: Size the passage from the facade rather than from the code. On a five-bay Georgian front the passage takes about a third of the width - 12 to 14 ft on a 42 to 48 ft front - and on a seven-bay front a fifth to a quarter. Southern vernacular passages run 8 to 12 ft because the passage is a room used in summer; northern vernacular passages run 6 to 7 ft because they are circulation and the heat is precious. The functional test is furnishability: a passage takes a 30 in deep case piece against one wall and still leaves 44 in clear, which puts the floor at 6 ft 2 in for a working minimum and 8 ft before it reads as a room. Below 5 ft the space cannot receive a visitor, which is the single social act the centre passage was invented to perform. Where area is genuinely short, take the width from the passage's LENGTH rather than its breadth - a passage two thirds of the depth opening into a rear stair hall is a documented plan and a corridor is not.

fixes.right: Draw the passage as a room, at 10-14 ft for a formal plan or 8-12 ft for southern vernacular, and take the area out of the depth of the flanking rooms rather than out of the passage.
fixes.cheap: Widen the passage at one point rather than along its length. A 4 ft corridor that opens to 9 ft for a 7 ft length at the stair, or at the mid-point where the doors face each other, reads as a hall and costs about 20 sq ft rather than 250. This is what a rear stair hall does in a period plan and it is the fix that actually gets built. Second free move: raise the passage ceiling or give the passage the only cornice in the house, which buys apparent width at zero plan cost.
fixes.dishonest: Calling a 4 ft corridor a 'gallery' and hanging pictures in it. A gallery is a room you stop in; you cannot stop in 48 inches with a door swinging into it, and hanging art in a space where nobody can stand back three feet is a claim rather than a use.

detection: In a plan, divide the passage width by the width of the narrowest room it serves: below about 0.4 the passage is a corridor. In a photograph taken along the hall, look at the door casings: in a true passage the casings on opposite sides do not appear to touch and there is wall between the door and the corner, and a corridor shows continuous casing with no wall face between openings. A third check that works from an elevation alone: on a five-bay front, measure the centre bay's share of the total width - a passage at a third of the frontage shows as a wide central bay, and a corridor plan shows five bays evenly spaced with the door bay no wider than the window bays.

test.note: 8 ft for a formal centre-passage plan and 6 ft for a northern vernacular one. The code floor of 3 ft is not a design value. Where only an elevation is available, use passage_bay_width / mean_window_bay_width, which should be at least 1.3.

exceptions.why: The First Period lobby-entrance plan has no passage at all - the front door opens onto the face of a central chimney four feet away, and the two tiny flanking spaces are stairs and turns, not a hall.
exceptions.bounds: Requires the central stack of 7 ft square or more and the winder stair in front of it. A 4 ft corridor beside a gable-end chimney is not a lobby entrance; it is a corridor.

exceptions.why: The full Cape's entry is a lobby against the stack with a boxed winder stair; the space is 4 to 6 ft square and is not pretending to be a room.
exceptions.bounds: Only where the chimney is central and the house is one-and-a-half storeys. A two-storey Cape Revival with a 4 ft centre corridor is the fault.

exceptions.why: A row-house side hall on a 16-25 ft lot cannot be a room; 4 to 5 ft is the historic dimension and the compensation is height, a 10-12 ft ceiling and an arched screen into the stair.
exceptions.bounds: Requires the narrow lot, the raised parlour floor and the compensating ceiling height. A 4 ft hall under an 8 ft ceiling on a 60 ft wide suburban lot has the constraint without the reason.

granted_when.note: The same licence covers Greek Revival and Federal urban rows.

exceptions.why: Deliberately hall-less. A hall added down one side converts the building to a side-hall cottage and is a different type.
exceptions.bounds: Overall width 12-16 ft with no interior hallway at all. This is an exception by absence, not a licence for a narrow one.

confused_with.difference: Width against ends. The two faults have the same driver and different geometry, and a plan very often has one or the other but rarely both, because the second one is what you do when the first one was refused.
That is about where the stair starts within the passage. A 14 ft wide passage with the stair rising immediately inside the door is still a stairwell.
Same driver in the vertical: circulation dimensioned from the code's life-safety floor rather than from the type. The two travel together because one plan review produces both.

severity_by_style.why: In the Chesapeake and the Deep South the passage is a summer room with doors at both ends; at 4 ft it has no function left at all.
The passage is the style's central social invention and a corridor is not a narrow version of it.
Northern passages are genuinely narrower - 6 to 8 ft is documented - so the gap between correct and endemic is smaller.
The type is built to a budget and a small hall is authentic to it.

sources: proportions/systems/room-vernacular.json circulation_parti derived rule and note
